title: Foundations of Trauma Neuroscience
subtitle: How threat, learning, memory and regulation interact
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating foundations of trauma neuroscience across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain foundations of trauma neuroscience in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in foundations of trauma neuroscience.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to foundations of trauma neuroscience.

sections.explainSimply: Trauma is not stored in one brain region; it reflects coordinated changes in threat detection, memory, arousal and regulation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: A trauma formulation links nervous-system state, learning history, appraisal, avoidance, attachment and context rather than reducing distress to a single circuit.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Research supports altered function across amygdala–hippocampal–prefrontal systems and large-scale networks, but findings are heterogeneous and not diagnostic at the individual level.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of foundations of trauma neuroscience as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need foundations of trauma neuroscience to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Group-level neuroimaging findings cannot determine whether one person has trauma.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use foundations of trauma neuroscience to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses foundations of trauma neuroscience to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Group-level neuroimaging findings cannot determine whether one person has trauma. Evidence classification: established systems framework; heterogeneous biomarkers.
